title: Developing a multiplayer extraction RTS using AI only: three lessons that had nothing to do with code (base prompt included)
author: idlerunner00
selftext:
I'm developing Out of Pixkrieg, a multiplayer extraction RTS that runs in the browser, and I'm doing it with AI only. That includes the art. There are no image models and no hand-drawn assets in it: every soldier, animal, flag, avatar, skill effect and map comes out of procedural generators that Claude Code (Opus 5.5) and Codex (GPT Astra) wrote in Rust.

The game in one paragraph: you own a roster of generated units, gear them up and send them into raids. On the map you loot, mine, free captives and fight bandits, AI parties and other players (PvPvE). Whoever you get out at an extraction point comes home, together with the loot. Whoever falls is gone for good. What makes it home goes into your camp and your units, and then you decide who goes out again.

Getting the code written works surprisingly well by now, so I'd rather share three things I learned outside of it.

**1. Build measurement in from day one and let the AI iterate on the numbers**

Before the first public playtest I had the agents build telemetry, a funnel and a small admin dashboard into the game. More important than the dashboard: design targets with a range, so every playtest gives a verdict instead of a feeling. A few of mine:

* first command within 10 s of entering a raid (measured: 8 s)
* tutorial takes 2 to 3 minutes (measured: 2.8)
* 15 to 20 % unit loss per raid (measured: 7.3 %)
* 40 to 60 % loss in the core, the most dangerous ring of the map (measured: 6 %, so my risk curve was upside down)
* median raid of at 15 minutes (measured: 13.6)

The funnel was a eye opener. About half of all players stopped in the tutorial. I would never have found that through feedback, because the people who quit don't write anything. I handed Claude the numbers, it reworked the tutorial (one thing at a time, clear next step, a coach), and in the current playtest about 70 % get through. That was one iteration. My hope is the next one closes more of the gap.

**2. A content pipeline, because I really don't like video editing**

To be honest, I'm bad at marketing material. Before this project I had never cut a clip and didn't have a single social media channel. So I had Claude build a devlog pipeline next to the game:

* the game has a deterministic scene studio that renders a staged scene from a seed, the same way every time
* the pipeline records it, cuts it on the words of the narration, adds the text and the music
* a local TTS model speaks the lines, Whisper checks that they were spoken right
* measurable QC: motion in the first frame, contrast, frozen frames, loudness, safe zones, hook length
* shorts, longer clips and before/after comparisons of two builds all come out of the same tools, and a campaign is basically a JSON file

The clip above came out of it. The results aren't perfect yet, but I have the start of a fully automated content pipeline that can run without a single API call if it has to. With AI on top (ideas, a final image review) the quality gets better, but it isn't required.

**3. Build the community into the game**

In my previous project, ExoSiege, the link to Discord was one of the things players liked most. So Out of Pixkrieg got it early: the in-game chat and Discord are one chat, and feedback written in the game becomes a thread in the Discord forum, with replies going back into the game. Instead of feedback in five places there is one place, and players who never join Discord still talk to the ones who do. This creates one common shared place and helps bringing players together that use different mediums.

**What the AI has built so far**

* procedural generators for units, animals, terrain, flags, avatars and skills (plus buildings, walkers, items, names, the pixel font and the sounds)
* working multiplayer in the browser with a base and a raid system
* authoritative servers, accounts, matchmaking, persistence, crash recovery
* the Discord bot, the playtest dashboard and the content pipeline

In numbers: about 5,700 commits and a bit over 200 architecture decision records since early October.

**Stack**

* Rust for everything: simulation, netcode, generators, renderer, UI, audio
* client: Rust on wgpu compiled to WASM, WebGPU with a WebGL2 fallback build, plus a thin TypeScript shell for loading, the canvas and browser APIs. The UI is drawn by the engine, with its own generated pixel font
* servers: a meta service (accounts, roster, camp, economy, matchmaking) and an authoritative raid host (fixed tick, WebTransport with WebSocket fallback, fog of war computed on the server so map hacks can't work, regular checkpoints so a crash costs less than a minute)
* Postgres, Redis, Docker Compose, Caddy, one rented server in Germany

Rust + WASM is probably the best combination I've used for vibe coding so far. The compiler and a strict clippy config catch a lot of what agents get wrong before anything runs, big refactors stay safe, and the same crates run natively in tests and in the browser. The pathfinding in the client is literally the server's code.

**Workflow**

Simple, really. Codex and Claude Code run as extensions in VS Code. I prompt orchestrators, and the actual work is mostly done by sub-agents the orchestrators steer. The orchestrators make sure one central rule set is followed: no duplicated code (jscpd breaks the build), no ready-made assets, clippy pedantic with warnings as errors, coverage and mutation testing thresholds, and an independent adversarial review before anything merges.

**It all started with one prompt**

Many, many prompts have gone into the iteration since, but it began with one very detailed prompt that produced the whole base in a single session over about 2 to 3 days. I can imagine that's interesting for some of you, so it follows at the bottom, translated from German with paths and machine details removed.

You can try the current version for free in the browser: [https://pixkrieg.com](https://pixkrieg.com)

\--------------

**Prompt:**

# Brief: production-ready browser RTS extraction game ("Tarkov as an RTS")

# 0. Brief and working mode

In this directory you build a complete, production-ready multiplayer game that runs **in the browser**. The whole stack runs on **Docker Compose**, locally and in production. Native desktop builds and Steam come **later** and are **not part of this brief**, but the architecture keeps the way open for them from the start (6.1).

**The bar is maximum quality in every discipline, without compromise:** code, architecture, performance, netcode, security, game design, graphics, UX, audio and operations. Section 4 applies to every line and every decision.

* You work **fully autonomously** until the Definition of Done (13) is met.
* You make routine decisions yourself, document them and keep working. You don't stop for questions; only section 14 defines exceptions.
* You start without prior knowledge. Everything relevant is in here, the reference repo is attached at the end.

**Environment:** Windows 11, PowerShell 5.1 and Git Bash, a 6-core desktop CPU, a high-end GPU, 64 GB RAM, MSVC build tools. Docker Desktop (Hyper-V) whose VM (\~12 GB) is shared with other permanently running stacks that occupy host ports, so resource limits and collision-free ports are mandatory. Toolchains are installed locally to the project, not system-wide.

# 1. Game concept (confirmed by the user)

* **Genre:** open-world RTS extraction, "Tarkov as an RTS". Full multiplayer with PvP.
* **Platform:** the browser now, so everyone can play right away. Later a native client and Steam from the same codebase with one shared player pool (not in this brief).
* **Raids:** session-based. A raid instance stays open 1–2 hours, players join and leave (join-in-progress).
* **On the map:** small bandit camps everywhere (PvE), mineable resource nodes (stone, wood, …), safe zones with shops where you recruit new people, extraction points where you extract with your people, PvP against other players and their armies.
* **Units:** every unit is procedurally generated and unique: look, role, gear, name.
   * Recruits hired in a raid are loot. They fight from the moment they are hired but only belong to the player after extraction.
   * Death means the unit is lost for good. The player can always start with 3 basic units, so a total loss is impossible.
   * "Unit bonbons" give random units. Rarity runs through the generator's tiers (Recruit, Veteran, Elite, Hero).
* **Lobby / base:** extracted units produce resources there passively, used to recruit and craft. The core tension: send people back into the risk, or let them produce safely.
* **Scale:** plan with really large numbers from the start. Massive armies are the baseline, not a later feature.
* **Hosting:** a rented server in Germany, ≈ 15 ms RTT from the user's machine.

Everything not fixed here you design yourself in `docs/GDD.md` along the pillars in section 2: crafting, items, loot tables, economy, progression, raid entry and end, factions, squads, map size, tutorial, social features. You justify each decision and balance by simulation and bot playtests.

# 2. Design pillars

1. **Risk versus reward:** every decision to take people along is felt.
2. **Every unit is precious:** procedural identity and permadeath create attachment.
3. **Readability at large scale:** figure before ground, squads, levels of detail when zooming out.
4. **Latency-proof by design:** channel times, announced abilities and server-side stances instead of reflex micro.
5. **Minimal, intuitive UI.**
6. **Fairness:** the server decides everything, no pay-to-win.

# 3. Golden rules (not negotiable)

1. Code is never duplicated, it is always abstracted properly, to keep it maintainable in the long run.
2. Ready-made assets are excluded. We use existing generators or build new ones. That includes terrain, fonts, sounds, music, icons and UI graphics.
3. Everything UI-related is as intuitive, minimalist and simple as possible, with a unique style that fits the 8-bit style of the figures.

**CI enforces the rules mechanically:** duplicate detection across Rust and TypeScript (e.g. `jscpd`) with a fixed threshold; a check of the module layers (section 7), so browser code outside the platform crates breaks the build; no image, audio or font files in the repo except generated test references in one folder; UI designed by hand but built in code from shared palette tokens, with frames in code, icons from generators and a custom pixel font as glyph data.

# 4. Quality bar: maximum, without exception

**The bar is the best commercial titles of the genre, not a good prototype.** "Works" does not mean "done". Something is done when it is excellent, measured and independently reviewed. If it feels "good enough", it is not done.

**Principles:**

* **No shortcuts on** `main`**,** checked by CI: no placeholders, mocks or stubs, no commented-out code, no `TODO`, `FIXME`, `todo!()`, `unimplemented!()`, no "later".
* **Every component is built as if the leading experts of its field were signing it off.**
* **For every important decision you examine at least two serious alternatives,** measure them where possible and record the result in an ADR.
* **Results below a gate are improved, not talked up.**
* **Simplicity is quality.** The simplest solution that meets all requirements excellently. No abstraction without benefit, no dependency without need.

**Technical gates in CI:**

* **Rust:** `rustfmt`; `clippy -D warnings` with selected pedantic lints; `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` by default (`unsafe` only with written justification, `SAFETY` comment and Miri tests); `#![deny(missing_docs)]` in all library crates.
* **TypeScript shell:** strict mode, lint without warnings. **Docker:** Dockerfiles linted (`hadolint`), Compose config validated.
* **Build:** zero warnings. **Flaky tests:** zero, a flaky test is a bug.
* **Coverage** ≥ 90 % of lines in foundation, generators, rules, net and meta (`cargo-llvm-cov`). That is the floor, not the goal.
* **Mutation testing** (`cargo-mutants`) for rules, economy, transactions and netcode, ≥ 90 % caught.
* **Property tests** for all invariants (resources are never duplicated, HP stay in bounds, transactions balance).
* **Fuzzing** (`cargo-fuzz`) of all decoders and parsers: network protocol, storage formats, generator specs. Regular CI runs, no open findings.
* **Supply chain:** `cargo-deny` (licences, advisories, duplicate versions), minimal pinned dependencies, pinned base images, reproducible builds.
* **Performance:** p50 and p99 budgets in CI, no frame over twice the budget in benchmark scenes, memory budgets and GPU times measured.

**Product gates through reviews:**

* **Scorecards** for graphics, UX, game feel, audio and game design, each at least **9/10**, scored by at least two independent reviewer subagents (a third decides on disagreement).
* **Game feel:** local feedback in the same frame, visual and audio feedback for every action, a clean pixel grid (integer scaling, no subpixel jitter, no blur).
* **Final panel:** one expert subagent per discipline (game design, art direction, rendering, simulation, netcode, security, UX, audio, operations). Each signs off with at least 9/10; all findings are fixed or justified in an ADR.

# 5. Starting material: reference repo (read only)

Attached at the end is the repo with the **unit and structure generator**, the only starting material. Everything else is built new, terrain included. **It is never modified;** for reference runs you copy it into a git-ignored cache directory.

* Godot 4.5 .NET / C#, engine-independent core, golden tests, console harness. Read README and `docs/` first: the style decisions actually made are written there.
* Painting logic: a canvas of material and tone step instead of colours; 5-step OKLCH ramps whose shadows shift to blue-violet (285°) and highlights to warm yellow (85°); one global outline colour `Oklch(0.215, 0.038, 282)`; light from the top left, volume shading per shape; earthy materials, only team and gem colours saturated.
* Measured: body median 14 px (18 px with weapon, 17 px wide); 148 frames per atlas (5 clips × 3 stored directions, west mirrored); \~34 ms per unit (native, one core); \~7 KB download (Brotli) with palette index. A name generator exists.

**Port:** unit, item, name and structure generators are reimplemented in Rust and **checked bit-exact against the C# originals**: the C# harness produces reference hashes (e.g. `ContentHash` of all frames for ≥ 10k seeds), which Rust must match exactly, natively and in the WASM build. After that, Rust is canonical. Bugs in the originals go into `docs/UPSTREAM_ISSUES.md` instead of being fixed there.

# 6. Technical architecture

This direction was analysed on 2026-10-03 with performance as the top criterion and partly measured. Validate it first with spikes (M1). If a measurement refutes a decision, choose the better alternative and justify it in an ADR.

**Rejected:**

|Option|Reason|
|:-|:-|
|Godot|no stable C# web export, WebGL2 only, large downloads|
|three.js|3D engine, wrong tool for 2D pixel sprites|
|PixiJS|the scene graph becomes the bottleneck with massive armies|
|TypeScript renderer with DOM UI|a later native/Steam client would rewrite renderer and UI, violates rule 1|
|Node server|same kernel 1.4–1.7× slower than C#, hard to parallelise|
|Lockstep|trivial map hacks, the slowest player slows everyone, determinism across browsers unreliable|

# 6.1 Overview

* **One Rust codebase for everything:** simulation, netcode, generators, renderer, UI, audio logic.
* **Server:** Rust, authoritative, split into the meta service (`meta`) and the raid host (`raid`).
* **Client:** Rust on `wgpu`, compiled to WASM. WebGPU with WebGL2 as fallback, shaders in WGSL. Plus a **thin TypeScript shell** for loading, canvas, browser APIs and a hidden input field for text, IME and clipboard.
* **Platform layer:** window/canvas, input, network transport, audio output, storage and login sit behind traits. Only the browser implementation exists for now. Engine and game crates stay platform-neutral (tests run natively), so a native client or Steam becomes an extra target instead of a port.
* **Persistence:** Postgres. Volatile state in Redis.

# 6.2 Simulation

* Every raid instance is its own process under the raid host, with a data-oriented ECS, a fixed 10–20 Hz tick and a job system across all cores.
* Movement and combat: spatial grid, staggered target search, separation; units in melee are anchored.
* **Pathfinding:** shared flowfields per squad target, hierarchical over portals, computed asynchronously.
* **Vision:** one vision grid per team, updated incrementally; structures and cliffs block sight.
* **Control:** squads and formations are the basic element of control and replication; individual control stays possible for small groups.
* **Measured** (C# prototype without pathfinding and vision, 12 threads): 50k units 5.4 ms per tick, 100k units 9.2 ms (p99 17 ms). Expect 2–3× with all features.
* **Raid state** is saved to Postgres every 30–60 s and resumed automatically after a crash: 1–2 h of player investment and permadeath are at stake.

# 6.3 Netcode

* **Curve replication** after Planetary Annihilation instead of snapshots: a segment is start point, velocity and start time; attacks, hits and deaths are events.
* **Interest management:** the server only sends what is visible. Fog of war is computed server-side, so map hacks are impossible. Full precision in the viewport, reduced beyond, only squad data when zoomed out.
* **Tolerance** 2 px, corrections blended in smoothly.
* **Measured** per 1000 units in a field battle: curves ≈ 15 KB/s plus 2 KB/s events, versus 53–78 KB/s for snapshots.
* **Transport:** WebTransport with separate streams and datagrams, WebSocket as a full fallback, both tested equally. Binary, quantised protocol with keyframes for join-in-progress and resumption.

# 6.4 Latency design

**Goal:** instant up to 150 ms RTT, fully playable up to 500 ms.

* **Local and instant:** camera, selection, UI, command markers, confirmation animation.
* **Predicted:** own squads start moving immediately, with the same pathfinding as the server, in the client as WASM. The server evaluates commands from the client's timestamp, capped at 250–300 ms, so prediction and server agree.
* **Authoritative:** damage, deaths, loot, shop, extraction.
* **Attack wind-ups hide latency:** melee 275–305 ms to the hit frame, ranged 490–580 ms plus flight time. A late message makes the client enter the animation later.
* **Design rules:** channel times at least as long as the RTT budget (loot, mining, extraction 10–30 s); abilities announced at least 0.5 s in advance; server-side stances (retreat at X % HP, keep distance, focus) compensate for reaction time.

**Latency emulator from day 1** with four profiles: EU 20 ms; overseas 150 ms, 1 % loss; far away 300 ms, 2 % loss, ±50 ms jitter; worst case 500 ms, 2 % loss, ±100 ms jitter. Acceptance at 500 ms: no freezing, no visible correction over 4 px, own units move in the frame the command is given, fights stay readable.

# 6.5 Client and renderer (Rust on wgpu, WASM)

* **GPU-driven:** every unit is one entry in a GPU buffer (curve, clip, clip start, direction, design, palette row, flags). The vertex shader computes position and frame; the CPU only writes on events.
* **Palette-index atlases** (R8) in texture arrays plus a palette texture. Team colour, hit flash and dithered fade run in the shader: \~75 KB of graphics memory instead of \~294 KB RGBA per unit.
* **Depth test instead of Y sorting** (binary transparency): all units in one draw call, shadows in their own pass, occlusion by structures and cliffs through their depth.
* **WebGL2 fallback** within `wgpu`'s WebGL2 feature set; data textures where storage buffers are missing; shader variants generated from one source, never written twice.
* **Massive armies:** infantry shares designs per squad or type (64–256 per raid), variety through a palette row per unit, heroes stay individual, a strategic zoom level shows banners or dots.
* **Threads:** one thread plus web workers where measured useful. SharedArrayBuffer only if measurements require it (ADR), since COOP/COEP headers make embedding harder.
* **WASM size** measured against the load budget from the start. **Browsers:** current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari on desktop.

# 6.6 Generators and content

All generators are written in Rust, and every module gets a workshop web app.

* **Foundation:** deterministic maths (bit-exact), seed streams, StableHash, noise, OKLCH, ramps and style as data, material canvas, painter, palette-index sprite and atlas format, encoder.
* **Units**, items (weapons, gear, inventory icons) and names, plus **structures** (parts and sites), ported (section 5): bandit camps by difficulty, safe zones with shop and recruiter, extraction points. Every structure provides collision, vision blockers, depth, shadow and anchor slots.
* **Terrain:** new, our own, minimalist (6.7).
* **Flora and props including resource nodes, new:** one generator for decorative and mineable objects (trees, bushes, rocks, ore). Mineable means a flag, depletion stages and a readability signal. Same painting logic as the units.
* **Map layout, new, gameplay first:** camps by difficulty, resource fields, safe zones, extraction points, fair spawns, paths and chokepoints; terrain fills nature in around them. Validators check reachability per size class, spawn fairness, the risk gradient and access to extraction points.
* **Maps:** generated, validated pools rotated per season, so map knowledge becomes skill as in Tarkov; fresh seeds per raid stay a technical option. Client and server generate the map from seed and spec, there are no map downloads. Changes such as mined nodes or destroyed gates are network events.
* **Pixel font, audio and icons:** all generated. Effects by synthesis, music generative or composed in code, output through WebAudio behind the platform layer.

# 6.7 Terrain: our own, minimalist generator

**Goal:** a calm, instantly readable ground against which thousands of units stand out. Minimalism is a quality goal, not a budget measure: few elements, each executed perfectly.

* **Style from the units:** same painting logic, always less contrast and saturation than the figures, never team hues.
* **Large calm areas instead of noise:** few ground materials per biome (grass, earth/path, sand, rock, marsh). Details are sparingly drawn motifs (grass tufts, pebbles, flowers) on a world-fixed grid, chosen by a hash per cell from designed variants. Noise never colours individual pixels.
* **Height as gameplay:** about 3–5 discrete levels with cliff faces in the unit style and clear ramps, which create readable chokepoints. Cliffs block movement; you define the vision rules for height in the GDD.
* **Water:** lakes, rivers, fords. Shallow water is slow, deep water impassable. Animation only by palette cycling.
* **Transitions:** clean pixel edges with minimum run lengths, at most one dither band between two materials.
* **Biomes** are palette and flora sets, not algorithms of their own.
* **Rendering in chunks:** a compact material map plus a shader that derives pixel details deterministically from world coordinates, no large baked textures, the same palette-index and LUT principle as the units, few draw calls per chunk.
* **Semantic output:** walkability per size class, movement cost, height level, vision blockers, water depth, site suitability.
* **Deterministic and seamless across chunk borders,** with golden tests, and publishable on its own as "Terrain + Flora".

# 6.8 Backend, meta, persistence

* **Meta service:** accounts (choose and justify the method, e.g. passkeys with email fallback; the login interface lets providers such as Steam dock on later), roster, storage, base, crafting, shop, bonbons, starter units, matchmaking, raid orchestration (assignment to raid hosts), seasons.
* **Passive resources** are computed from timestamps on request, nothing runs continuously.
* **Value transactions** (extraction, death, purchase) are server-side, atomic and idempotent, so nothing can be duplicated.
* **Migrations** are versioned, run idempotently at startup and are tested.
* **GDPR:** data minimisation, a deletion concept, self-hosted privacy-friendly telemetry.

# 6.9 Docker, hosting and operations

The stack follows a proven sister project of the user's and is fully described here.

**Ports** (deliberately non-standard, configurable in `.env`): 5886/tcp `client` (static web client, workshops under `/workshop/<name>/`, nginx), 5887/tcp `meta` (`/api/*`, `/health`), 5888/tcp `raid` (WebSocket fallback `/ws`, `/health`), 5888/udp `raid` (WebTransport, HTTP/3 over QUIC). Postgres and Redis are on the internal network only; optional debug ports are commented out and bind only to `127.0.0.1`.

**Services** in `docker-compose.yml`, with a top-level `name:`, containers named `<codename>_<service>`, a bridge network and a named Postgres volume:

|Service|Content|
|:-|:-|
|`db`|`postgres:16-alpine` (pinned), volume, healthcheck `pg_isready`|
|`redis`|`redis:7-alpine` for volatile state (sessions, matchmaking queue, raid registry, presence, rate limits); durable state only in Postgres|
|`meta`|Rust meta service, migrations at startup|
|`raid`|Rust raid host: starts and supervises raid processes, terminates WebTransport and WebSocket, saves raid states, writes a last checkpoint on `SIGTERM`|
|`client`|multi-stage build (WASM + TypeScript shell) → static files in `nginx:alpine`|

**Compose conventions:**

* A shared `x-logging` anchor (json-file, 10 MB, 3 files) on every service.
* Resource limits on every service (`cpus`, `memory`, `pids`), because the Docker VM is shared and a runaway service must never starve the others. Starting values to measure and adjust: db 1 CPU / 1 GB, redis 0.5 / 512 MB, meta 2 / 1 GB, raid 6 / 4 GB, client 0.5 / 128 MB.
* `init: true` for the Rust services, `restart: unless-stopped`, `stop_grace_period` ≥ 30 s for `raid`.
* `depends_on` **only with** `service_started`**, never** `service_healthy`**:** on this host, health-driven start orchestration hangs sporadically. Services wait for DB and Redis themselves with capped exponential backoff.
* Healthchecks in the Dockerfiles, minimal non-root runtime images, a `healthcheck` subcommand in the Rust binary where there is no shell.
* A git-ignored `.env` with a complete, commented `.env.example` (secrets, CORS origin, never `*`, log level, limits, ports, public URLs). In production the servers refuse to start with default secrets.

**Builds:** Dockerfiles under `docker/` (BuildKit, repo root as context). Rust multi-stage with a pinned toolchain, cached dependency layer, LTO and `codegen-units = 1`, only the binary in the runtime image. Client: Rust → `wasm32-unknown-unknown` → `wasm-bindgen` (exact crate version) → `wasm-opt`, shell through pnpm `--frozen-lockfile`. nginx serves precompressed files with the correct `application/wasm` type, fingerprinted assets as `immutable` and `index.html` as `no-store`, so a deploy always serves the fresh entry document.

`scripts/stack.ps1` is the only supported way to start the stack locally, because `docker compose up` hangs sporadically on this host while create and single `docker start` work reliably. `up [-Build]` checks the ports first (abort if a foreign process owns one), builds images one at a time, runs `docker compose create`, then starts each container in dependency order and waits for `healthy` with a timeout. Plus `down`, `restart` and `status`.

**WebTransport and TLS:** locally the raid host makes a short-lived self-signed ECDSA certificate and the meta service hands its hash to the client (`serverCertificateHashes`), with the WebSocket fallback where unsupported. In production the raid host terminates QUIC/TLS itself (ACME). Check whether a reverse proxy can forward WebTransport instead of assuming it.

**Local development without Docker:** `cargo run` for `meta` and `raid` (in-memory store without `DATABASE_URL`), a client dev server with hot reload.

**Production:** the same Compose files plus `docker-compose.prod.yml`, Caddy on the host as TLS proxy, a DNS-only realtime host (never behind a CDN) for `/ws`, WebTransport directly to the raid host. Raid hosts are root servers with dedicated cores that register with the meta service. Infrastructure as code, deploy and rollback scripts, backups with a tested restore, an `observability` profile, alerts and runbooks.

# 7. Repo and module structure

A monorepo with strict layers, **foundation ← generators ← engine ← game**, platforms only at the edge.

    crates/foundation/    maths, style/colour ramps, grids, sprite format
    crates/generators/    units, items, names, structures, flora, terrain, world, font, audio
    crates/engine/        render (wgpu), ui, audio, input, platform (traits only)
    crates/platform/      web (WASM bindings, WebTransport/WebSocket, WebAudio, input)
    crates/game/          rules, sim, net, meta-server, raid-server, client
    apps/                 game, unit-, structure- and world-workshop (web)
    web/shell/            thin TypeScript shell
    docker/ deploy/ scripts/ tools/ docs/

* **Generators never know game code,** they exchange only data and interfaces (e.g. sites provide tagged slots, the game decides who stands in them).
* **Engine and game code know no platform.** Everything browser-specific lives in `crates/platform/web`; a later `native` or `steam` platform is added without restructuring.
* **Style is an input value** (a preset from the foundation), not code.
* **One output format for all generators,** so there is one renderer, one atlas packer and one exporter.
* **Every generator module is publishable on its own,** with its own build, tests, README, CHANGELOG, semver, licence and workshop. Generators can be licensed separately, the game code is proprietary; you propose the licence in `docs/NEEDS_USER.md`.

# 8. Scaling and performance targets

The baseline, not a ceiling. If measurements allow, you go higher.

|Area|Target|
|:-|:-|
|Raid|64 players, 50,000 simulated units in total|
|Server tick|p99 < 50 ms at 20 Hz with all features on 8 dedicated cores (proven locally in the `raid` container with its CPU limit)|
|Client|60 fps with 5,000 visible animated units on an Intel Iris Xe class iGPU|
|Renderer stress test|100k instances|
|Terrain|whole map semantics on the server < 2 s; visible area in the client < 300 ms; p99 per chunk ≤ 25 ms in WASM|
|Bandwidth per client|typically < 30 KB/s, large-battle peak < 100 KB/s|
|Loading|< 5 MB to the lobby including WASM, lobby in < 3 s on broadband|
|Stack|cold start via `stack.ps1 up` without build ≤ 30 s to all `healthy`|
|Stability|2-h bot raids without memory growth, < 60 s lost after a crash|

The CPU's integrated graphics, set to "Power saving" per browser in Windows, serve as the low-end reference.

# 9. Art, UI, audio

* **One art bible for the whole game.** The units set the style; structures, terrain, flora, icons and UI follow with the same painting logic. Principles: **figure before ground** (units always stand out), **drawn, not noisy** (every pixel belongs to a designed shape), **breathing palette** (light, water and fire animate through ramps, not blur). It covers projection, pixel density, ramps, outline rules, contrast budgets, reserved team hues, state signals (mineable, danger, safe zone, extraction) and readability at every zoom level.
* **Team colours** are colour-blind-safe and also distinguished by shapes.
* **UI in the Rust renderer:** palette tokens, custom pixel font, frames in code, integer scaling, minimal and diegetic where it makes sense, rebindable shortcuts, German and English.
* **Input:** mouse and keyboard; the input layer can take gamepads later without restructuring.
* **Onboarding:** a tutorial raid that teaches the core loop in a few minutes.
* **Audio:** procedural, with mix priorities for massive battles, so no wall of sound builds up.

# 10. Quality assurance

On top of the gates in section 4:

* **Tests:** unit, property and golden tests including determinism and parity with the C# originals (natively and in WASM); integration tests against the Docker stack; headless bot clients for load and gameplay; an economy simulation for balancing; replays from the curves; latency emulator and soak tests; crash tests (e.g. `docker kill` of the raid container mid-raid); security tests (authorisation, input validation, rate limits, duplication attempts).
* **Browser tests** with Playwright in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit against the Docker stack, over WebTransport and WebSocket.
* **Benchmarks** with budgets in CI; regressions break the build.
* **Visual reviews** only in subagents, never in the main session: at most \~10 cropped or downscaled images per subagent, at most 2–3 such subagents at once, always with a concrete question, because the user's upload bandwidth is limited and shared.
* **Code reviews:** a separate adversarial review before every merge into `main` (correctness, security, performance, maintainability); findings are fixed before merging.

# 11. Way of working and autonomy

* **Start:** read the reference repo, then write `docs/VISION.md`, `GDD.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `ART_BIBLE.md`, `QUALITY.md` (gates, scorecards, budgets) and `ROADMAP.md`.
* **Progress:** `docs/PROGRESS.md` (status, next steps, open risks) and `docs/adr/` (decisions), always up to date, so work continues seamlessly after a context summary. Read `PROGRESS.md` at the start of every work phase.
* **Decisions** in this order: golden rules > correctness and security > quality > performance > effort. Effort is never a reason for the worse solution.
* **Subagents and multi-agent workflows** are explicitly allowed, to build in parallel and to review independently and adversarially.
* **Docker discipline:** stack only through `scripts/stack.ps1`, never `docker compose up`; never touch foreign containers and stacks; leave the stack in a defined state.
* **Git:** small clean commits on feature branches, merge into `main` after green checks and a passed review. No push, no remote, no publication without explicit approval.
* **Honesty:** report only measured results, call nothing done that is not tested, document failures with their output. A sugar-coated result is worse than an openly named problem.
* **No stopping halfway:** don't ask whether to continue. Stop only when the Definition of Done is met or only section 14 items remain.

# 13. Definition of Done

* **The Docker stack** starts reproducibly with `scripts/stack.ps1 up -Build`, all containers `healthy`, the game at `http://localhost:5886`, other stacks untouched.
* **The game loop runs end to end in the browser:** account, base, raid entry, raid with camps, nodes, safe zones, PvP and extraction, the result saved, and the loop starts over.
* **All section 8 targets** met as measured, latency acceptance at 500 ms passed.
* **All section 4 gates** met, all scorecards and the final panel at least 9/10.
* **Golden rules** enforced mechanically, without violations.
* **Open for native and Steam:** browser code only in `crates/platform/web`.
* **Ready to deploy:** staging succeeded, backups with a tested restore, only `docs/NEEDS_USER.md` items missing.
* **Generator modules** (units, structures, terrain + flora, map layout) are publishable on their own.
* **An honest final report:** what is done, what is measured, which weaknesses remain, what you recommend.

# 14. Limits of autonomy

You don't do the following yourself. You prepare them completely, list them in `docs/NEEDS_USER.md` and keep working on everything else:

spending money, signing contracts, creating third-party accounts;

working with credentials and secrets, deploying to public servers, pushing to remotes, publishing anything;

real-money monetisation (out of scope without an explicit order);

native builds and Steam (not part of this brief);

changes to the reference repo and to foreign Docker stacks;

game name and brand: you work with the neutral codename Exfil.
